 The short version: buy the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 , because 80% capacity after 4,000 cycles is the best longevity figure published for any portable unit here and it arrives in a 24.9 lb box that does 2,000W. If weight is what decides your purchase, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is 45.0Wh per pound — but read its cycle rating twice, because it is quoted to a different threshold. 
 That threshold is the whole reason this page exists. LiFePO4 has become the default chemistry across every mainstream brand, so "LiFePO4" on a box has stopped being a differentiator and started being a given. What still differs — enormously — is what the manufacturer promises the cells will still hold at the end of the rated cycle count. 
 Why the headline cycle number misleads
 Two units both advertise 4,000 cycles. One means 4,000 cycles to 80% of original capacity, the other means 4,000 cycles to 70%. Those are not the same claim. The second unit is allowed to lose half again as much capacity over the same number of charges, and both brands print "4,000 cycles" in the same size type. 
 Manufacturer-published chemistry and cycle figures, with the retention threshold stated as the manufacturer states it. Watt-hours per pound is our arithmetic. Unit Capacity Cycle rating Weight Wh per lb

 Read that table as a ranking of claims rather than of products. Anker's C1000 Gen 2 and EcoFlow's DELTA 3 Plus make the strongest promise: 4,000 cycles against the stricter 80% bar. BLUETTI makes fewer cycles at the same bar. Jackery makes the same cycle count at an easier bar. Anker's F3800 publishes a cycle count with no bar at all, which is the least useful version of the spec. 
 What a cycle count actually buys you
 4,000 cycles in calendar years
 Weekend camping, roughly two full cycles a week: 4,000 / 104 = 38 years 
 Van life, one full cycle a day: 4,000 / 365 = 11 years 
 Home UPS standby, maybe 20 real cycles a year: 4,000 / 20 = 200 years 
 In every case the calendar age of the cells, not the cycle count, becomes the limit 
 For anything short of daily deep cycling, the cycle rating is not the spec that will end the unit's life. Buy on weight, output and warranty instead. 
 This is the part most chemistry roundups leave out, and it changes the shopping advice completely. If you camp eight weekends a year, a 3,000-cycle unit and a 4,000-cycle unit will both outlive your interest in the hobby. The cycle rating only becomes the deciding spec if the unit cycles close to daily — a van build, an off-grid cabin, a shop that runs tools off a battery. How long portable power stations last covers the calendar-ageing side, which is the real limit for everyone else. 
 What LiFePO4 is genuinely better at
 Against the NMC chemistry that dominated this category five years ago, LFP wins on three things that matter here: cycle life by a factor of three or more, thermal stability, and tolerance of being left at a high state of charge. It loses on energy density, which is why an LFP unit is heavier than an NMC unit of the same capacity. LiFePO4 vs NMC power station batteries is the full comparison. 
 What LFP is not better at is cold. Below freezing the usable fraction of any lithium battery shrinks, and charging a LiFePO4 cell below 0°C is the one thing that genuinely damages it — which is why every unit here has a battery management system that refuses to. If your trips are winter trips, power stations in cold weather matters more to your purchase than the cycle rating does. 
 How to choose between these five
 You carry it — Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, at 45.0Wh per pound. Accept the 70% threshold. 
 You want the longest honest life — Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2: 80% after 4,000 cycles. 
 You run many small things in one place — BLUETTI AC180: 1,152Wh and four AC outlets. 
 You need it under 11 lb — EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus: 286Wh, 600W out, expands to 858Wh. 
 You are backing up a house — Anker SOLIX F3800: 3,840Wh, 6,000W, true 240V. 
 You are running panels — the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus takes 1,000W of solar, more than any unit above. 
 If you have not yet worked out your capacity requirement, do that before picking a chemistry: what size power station do I need takes five minutes and will usually move you a whole size band. And if expansion rather than longevity is your real concern, best expandable power stations ranks the same registry on that axis instead. 
 Two small units worth knowing about
 Below the capacities ranked above, the same chemistry argument plays out in miniature and the documentation gets noticeably thinner. The BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 publishes "over 3,000 cycles" on 288Wh of LiFePO4 — a real figure, but without the retention threshold that makes the claim comparable. The Anker SOLIX C300 , at the same capacity, publishes no cycle rating at all, which on an LFP unit is the gap we would want closed before buying on longevity. 
 A note on what we did not do
 We have not cycle-tested any of these units and we are not going to imply we have. Every cycle figure above is the manufacturer's own published claim, sourced below, and the only thing we have added is the arithmetic and the observation that the thresholds differ.  Questions
 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best LiFePO4 portable power station? + The Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2, on the strength of 80% capacity after 4,000 cycles — the best pairing of cycle count and retention threshold published for any portable unit here — delivered at 2,000W continuous from a 24.9 lb box. If weight is the deciding factor instead, the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is 45.0Wh per pound. 
 Are all portable power stations LiFePO4 now? + Every unit in this site's registry is, and LFP has become the mainstream default. That is exactly why the chemistry label on the box no longer separates products — the cycle rating and its retention threshold do. 
 How many cycles does a LiFePO4 power station last? + The units here publish between 3,000 and 4,000+ cycles. In calendar terms that is roughly 11 years at one full cycle a day, or decades at weekend-camping frequency, so for most buyers the cells' calendar age will end the unit's life before the cycle count does. 
 Why do some brands quote cycles to 70% and others to 80%? + Because the threshold is the manufacturer's choice and it is not standardised. Jackery quotes 4,000 cycles to 70% capacity; Anker, EcoFlow and BLUETTI quote to 80%. The same headline number against a looser bar is a weaker promise, and it is worth checking before comparing two spec sheets. 
 Is LiFePO4 better than NMC for a power station? + For this use case, yes — three times or more the cycle life, better thermal stability, and no harm from sitting at a high state of charge. The cost is energy density, so an LFP unit weighs more for the same capacity. Full comparison . 
 Does LiFePO4 work in cold weather? + It discharges in the cold with reduced usable capacity, but charging below freezing is genuinely damaging and every unit here has a battery management system that blocks it. If you camp in winter, read power stations in cold weather before buying.

 Frequently Asked Questions
 What size power station do I actually need for camping versus tailgating?
 For a solo or two-person weekend that charges phones, runs lights, and powers a fan, a 1kWh unit like the Anker SOLIX C1000 or Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is plenty and stays under 30 pounds. For a tailgate or group campsite that runs an electric grill, a cooler, and a full lighting rig, step up to a 2kWh unit like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 or Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. If you only charge devices and want to carry the unit in a daypack, the 286Wh EcoFlow River 3 Plus covers it.
 Can these run a coffee maker, electric grill, or mini-fridge?
 It depends on the continuous AC output, not the capacity. A mini-fridge draws roughly 60 to 100 watts and runs on any unit here. A coffee maker or kettle spikes to 1000 to 1500 watts, so you need at least the 1500W Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 and ideally an 1800W unit. An electric grill can pull 1500 to 2400 watts, which calls for the 2600W Bluetti Elite 200 V2 or the 2200W Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. Always check the appliance's running and surge wattage against the unit's continuous and peak ratings.
 How do I recharge one of these at a campsite or on the road?
 Three ways: a wall outlet at a campground hookup, a 12V car port while you drive, or a solar panel during the day. AC recharge is fastest, and the Anker SOLIX C1000 leads this group at 58 minutes to full, so a single overnight hookup tops it off. Car charging is slower and depends on your vehicle's port. Solar input ranges from 220W on the River 3 Plus to 1000W on the Elite 200 V2, so a panel is a daytime supplement for most of these rather than a primary recharge.
 Does LiFePO4 battery chemistry actually matter for a camping unit?
 Yes, for lifespan and safety. Every unit in this guide uses LiFePO4, also called LFP, which holds up for 3000 to 6000 charge cycles versus roughly 500 to 800 for the older NMC lithium in cheaper units. That is the difference between a decade of weekend use and a battery that fades in a few years. LiFePO4 also runs cooler and is more tolerant of being left partly charged, which suits gear that sits in a garage between trips. The tradeoff is slightly more weight per watt-hour, which these designs have largely engineered away.
 Can I fly with a power station or take one tailgating safely?
 You cannot fly with any of these. Airlines cap lithium batteries in carry-on at 100 watt-hours, with up to 160Wh by airline approval, and the smallest unit here is 286Wh, so all of them are far over the limit and barred from passenger flights. For driving to a tailgate or campsite they are perfectly safe: keep the unit ventilated, avoid leaving it in a hot sealed trunk for long stretches, and do not cover the cooling vents while it runs. LiFePO4 chemistry is among the most stable, which is part of why every pick here uses it.
 Is a solar panel worth buying with one of these?
 It depends on your trip length. For a weekend where you recharge at home before and after, a solar panel adds cost and bulk you may not need. For multi-day off-grid camping with no hookup, a panel is what keeps the unit alive, and the higher-input models like the Bluetti Elite 200 V2 at 1000W or the Anker C1000 at 600W make solar a real refill rather than a trickle, while the Jackery Explorers cap at 400W. Buy the panel sized to the unit's maximum solar input, and remember that real-world output runs well below the panel's rated wattage in anything but direct midday sun.

 Use DC for 12V gear

 Charge while you drive

 Keep it cool and dry
 Leave the station in the shade and out of the rain. Heat slows charging and wears the battery.
 Mind the cold

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 What is the best portable power station for camping? 
 For most campers, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 : 1,024Wh runs a 12V fridge for a long weekend, 2,000W handles camp cooking, and it recharges in 49 minutes from the wall or 1.8 hours from 600W of solar. If weight matters more, the EcoFlow RIVER 2 Pro (18.2 lb) or the RIVER 3 Plus (10.4 lb) are easier to carry. For CPAP users, the BLUETTI AC180 is our pick.
 What size power station do I need for camping? 
 For a weekend of phones, lights and a fan, 300 to 600Wh is enough. Add a 12V fridge or cooler and you want 700 to 1,200Wh. For a family, a multi-day trip or a nightly CPAP, look at 1,000 to 2,000Wh. Check your own gear with the power station calculator .
 How long will a power station run a camping fridge? 
 A 12V camping fridge averaging 45W runs about 5.5 hours on a 286Wh unit, about 15 hours on 768Wh, about 19 to 22 hours on a 1kWh-class unit and about 39 hours on 2,042Wh. Running the fridge from the 12V outlet rather than AC stretches that further, and so does keeping the fridge out of the sun. See our guide to camping fans and coolers .
 Can I run a CPAP machine while camping? 
 Yes. A CPAP drawing 40W for 8 hours uses about 320Wh, so a 1kWh-class station covers 2.5 to 3 nights and the 2,042Wh Explorer 2000 v2 about 5.5 nights. A humidifier or heated tube adds significantly to the draw. Running the CPAP on DC through a 12V outlet, as the BLUETTI AC180 allows, avoids inverter losses.
 How many times can a camping power station charge a phone or laptop? 
 Divide the usable capacity (about 85% of the rated watt-hours) by the device battery. Assuming a phone battery of about 15Wh and a laptop battery of about 60Wh, a 288Wh unit gives roughly 16 phone or 4 laptop charges, a 768Wh unit about 43 or 11, a 1,024Wh unit about 58 or 14, and the 2,042Wh Explorer 2000 v2 about 115 or 29.
 Can I run a heater or an electric blanket while camping? 
 A blanket, yes; a space heater, barely. A typical 1,500W space heater would drain a 1,024Wh station in about 35 minutes. A 12V heated blanket drawing around 50W, on the other hand, runs about 17 hours on the same unit. In cold weather, also remember that several of these stations can’t recharge below 32°F.
 Is a solar generator the same as a portable power station? 
 Almost. “Solar generator” is the marketing name for a portable power station sold with solar panels. The station stores and delivers the power; the panels recharge it. You can also buy the station alone and add compatible panels later.
 Can I charge a camping power station from my car? 
 Yes, all seven picks recharge from a 12V car socket. It is slow compared with a wall outlet (EcoFlow quotes about 3.3 hours for the 286Wh RIVER 3 Plus), but a day of driving adds meaningful energy between campsites.

 How much battery does a camping weekend need?
 Start with the cooler, because it runs all day. A 12V compressor cooler like the Dometic CFX3 45 averages about 13 W once it is cold, or about 312 Wh a day. Add a 100-count LED string for five hours (about 50 Wh) and charging two phones (about 48 Wh), and you are near 410 Wh a day.

 A box fan changes the math. At about 85 W for 8 hours, it adds about 680 Wh a night. With the fan running, the same 1,070 Wh station lasts about 20 hours instead of two days.
 What to look for in a camping power station
 Weight you will actually carry. Car campers can handle 25 lb. Walk-in sites and longer carries favor the 8.2 lb Jackery 300 v2 or the 10.4 lb RIVER 3 Plus.
 A 12V car-style socket. Most compressor coolers run on 12V. Plugging them into the station's car socket skips the inverter, which wastes roughly 10% to 15% of the battery as heat. Every pick here has one, so the cooler runtimes on this page are on the safe side.
 Solar input. On trips longer than a weekend, solar is how you keep going. The Elite 100 V2 takes up to 1,000 W, the Jackery 1000 v2 400 W, the RIVER 3 Plus 220 W, the Yeti 500 200 W and the Jackery 300 v2 100 W. Real panels rarely hit their rated watts, especially in shade or cloud.
 Battery type and cold. All five picks use LiFePO4 batteries rated for 3,000 to 4,000 cycles. Cold slows charging on lithium batteries, so keep the station in the tent or car on cold nights.
 Mistakes to avoid
 Running the cooler on AC through its wall adapter. Use the 12V cord instead and you get more hours from the same battery.
 Leaving the station in a hot car or in full sun all day. Heat ages lithium batteries. Keep it in the shade, even while it charges from panels.
 Expecting to run a space heater. A 1,500 W heater is beyond most picks, and even on the Jackery 1000 v2 it would empty the battery in a little over an hour. A 150 W electric blanket uses about 600 Wh a night and is a much better choice on the bigger units.
 Forgetting to charge before you leave. Top it up at home the night before, so you start the trip at 100%.
 Safety at camp
 Battery stations burn no fuel, so they are safe in a tent or camper, unlike a generator or a gas heater. Keep them off wet ground, out of the rain and with space around the vents. The Yeti 500's IPX4 rating means it handles splashes, not puddles or downpours.
 If you use a CPAP while camping, a power station should not be your only backup for therapy you cannot skip. Bring enough battery for an extra night, and talk to your supplier about backup options if you need it every night.
 Making a charge last longer
 Pre-chill the cooler at home on wall power, and keep it in the shade at camp. A full cooler holds its cold better than a half-empty one, and every lid opening makes the compressor run.
 Charge phones and lights from USB ports, and turn off the AC outlets when nothing needs them, since an idle inverter still draws power. Set out solar panels early in the day and turn them toward the sun as it moves.
 If you sleep with a CPAP, turn the humidifier off. At about 7 W, even the Jackery 300 v2 runs one for about four nights.
 Common questions
 What size power station do I need for camping? For a weekend with a 12V cooler, lights and phones, about 1,000 Wh. That load uses about 410 Wh a day, so a 1,070 Wh unit lasts about two days. For one night, or a trip without a cooler, a 300 to 500 Wh unit is enough. 
 How long will a power station run a 12V fridge or cooler? A compressor cooler like the Dometic CFX3 45 averages about 13 W once cold. A 288 Wh station runs it for about 19 hours, a 499 Wh station for about 33 hours and a 1,070 Wh station for about 70 hours. Hot weather and frequent lid opening cut those numbers. 
 Can I run a CPAP while camping on a power station? Yes. With the humidifier off, a CPAP uses about 7 W, so a 288 Wh unit lasts about four 8-hour nights. With the heated humidifier and tube on, it uses about 34 W, and a 1,070 Wh unit lasts about three nights. 
 Can a camping power station run a fan all night? A 20-inch box fan uses about 85 W. A 1,070 Wh unit runs one for about 11 hours, while a 286 Wh unit lasts about 3 hours. A small USB fan uses far less. 
 Can I charge a power station with solar panels while camping? Yes. Every pick takes solar, from 100 W on the Jackery 300 v2 (through USB-C) up to 1,000 W on the Elite 100 V2. Expect less than the panels' rating in real conditions, especially in shade or clouds. 
 Is a power station better than a generator for camping? For small loads, yes. It has no engine, needs no fuel and can run inside a tent. A generator is better for big loads like a 10,000 BTU portable air conditioner, which would drain a 1,024 Wh station in a little over an hour.

How much battery do you need, and how much can you carry?

Start with a simple camping day. Two phones charging for about two hours each use about 48 Wh. LED string lights for five hours use about 50 Wh. Two hours of laptop charging adds about 78 Wh. That is about 176 Wh a day, or about 207 Wh of battery once you allow for inverter losses.

So a 288 Wh unit covers that day with a little to spare, and a two-night weekend needs about 415 Wh, which points to the 499 Wh Yeti 500. Add a CPAP with the heated humidifier at about 272 Wh a night, and each day needs about 530 Wh of battery. That is where the 1,000 Wh class, at about 24 to 25 lb, earns its weight.

A fair rule: if you only charge small gadgets, carry the 8 to 10 lb units. If you sleep with a CPAP or want to run a cooler or mini fridge, the extra 15 lb of a 1,000 Wh unit is worth it.

What to look for in a light unit

Compare watt-hours per pound, not just weight. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 carries about 45 Wh per pound and the Anker C1000 Gen 2 about 41. The Jackery Explorer 300 v2 is about 35, the Yeti 500 about 31 and the RIVER 3 Plus about 28.

All five picks use LiFePO4 cells rated for 3,000 to 4,000 cycles. NMC packs can be a bit lighter for the same capacity, but they are usually rated for far fewer cycles. For a unit you will drain and refill on every trip, LiFePO4 is the better long-term buy.

Check surge if you want to run anything with a motor. A compact fridge needs about 500 W for a second at start-up, which the 600 W surge of the Explorer 300 v2 can handle. A full-size fridge needs about 1,000 W, which rules out the 300 v2 but not the 1,000 Wh picks.

Recharge speed matters when you are between campsites. The C1000 Gen 2 refills in about 49 minutes with UltraFast on, the RIVER 3 Plus in about an hour, the Explorer 300 v2 in about 76 minutes, the Yeti 500 in about 90 minutes in High input mode and the Explorer 1000 v2 in about 95 minutes.

Mistakes to avoid

Buying the smallest unit and then adding a CPAP is the most common mistake. A 288 Wh unit runs a CPAP with the heated humidifier for about 7 hours, just short of a full night.

Expecting a small unit to run kitchen gear is another. A drip coffee maker pulls about 1,000 W, so it needs a station with at least that much continuous output. The 300 W Explorer 300 v2 and 500 W Yeti 500 cannot run one.

Finally, remember that expansion batteries add weight. The RIVER 3 Plus is 10.4 lb on its own, but carrying an extra battery means carrying two boxes.

Safety

Keep the station dry and give it room to breathe. IPX4 on the Yeti 500 means it handles splashes, not being left in the rain or set in a puddle. Do not leave any of these in a hot car, since heat shortens battery life.

If you rely on a CPAP or oxygen, a small power station should never be your only backup for life-support equipment. Carry a second plan, and ask your doctor or equipment supplier what they recommend.

Making it last longer

Turning off the CPAP's heated humidifier and tube is the biggest saving on this page: draw drops from about 34 W to about 7 W, so a 288 Wh unit goes from about 7 hours to about four nights.

Charge phones and laptops from USB-C instead of the AC outlet, which skips inverter losses. Between trips, store the station partly charged in a cool, dry place and top it up every few months.

Common questions
What is the lightest power station that can run a CPAP?
The Jackery Explorer 300 v2 at 8.2 lb runs a CPAP without the humidifier for about four nights (about 35 hours). With the heated humidifier and tube on, it lasts about 7 hours, just short of a full night. For that, step up to the 16.1 lb Yeti 500, which lasts about 12 hours.
How heavy is a 1,000 Wh power station?
Most current 1,000 Wh class units weigh about 24 to 28 lb. The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 is 23.8 lb, the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 24.9 lb, the BLUETTI Elite 100 V2 25 lb and the EcoFlow DELTA 3 Plus 27.6 lb. The older BLUETTI AC180 is heavier at 35.3 lb.
Can a small power station run a mini fridge?
Yes, if its surge rating is at least about 500 W. The Jackery Explorer 300 v2, with a 600 W surge rating, runs a compact fridge for about 8 hours, and the Yeti 500 for about 14 hours. A full-size fridge needs about 1,000 W of surge, which rules out the 300 v2.
Is a 300 Wh power station enough for camping?
For phones, lights and a laptop, yes. A typical camp day of two phone charges, string lights for five hours and two hours of laptop charging uses about 176 Wh, so 288 Wh lasts nearly a day and a half. Add a CPAP with a humidifier or a fan and you need a bigger unit.
Are lighter power stations less durable?
Not on this list. All five picks use LiFePO4 batteries rated for 3,000 to 4,000 cycles. Jackery rates its cycle life to 70% capacity rather than 80%, so compare those numbers carefully.
